Antalya, Turkey. Sunday night. The longest climate summit ever held is two days past its deadline. Nearly two hundred countries are in the room.
Then the president of the summit says: I understand that there is no agreement on this text. And the main deal of the summit is gone.
Now, here's the strange part. Almost forty years ago, the same world faced a danger in the sky. And it agreed. In the end, every single country on Earth signed up.
Spray cans, fridges, air conditioners, all changed. And today, a hole that once opened over Antarctica is slowly closing.
By the end of this video, you'll know why the ozone deal worked, why climate is so much harder, and what that one success says about what could work next.
So, why could the world fix one problem in the sky, but not the other?
Chapter one. One voice is enough.
At a United Nations climate summit, there's no final vote. Not one.
The climate treaty has one hundred and ninety-eight members. One hundred and ninety-seven countries, plus the European Union.
Back in nineteen ninety-five, at the very first summit in Berlin, they couldn't agree on how to vote. The rule about voting was left in brackets. It's still in brackets today.
So every decision is made by consensus. In theory, one country, out of one hundred and ninety-eight, can stop a deal.
That's what happened in Copenhagen, in two thousand and nine. A handful of countries objected, and the summit could only take note of its own accord.

And in Antalya, it happened again, from two sides. The European Union, the U K, and small island nations refused a text that didn't even mention fossil fuels. Reports say Saudi Arabia, speaking for the Arab Group, and Russia, resisted phasing them out.
The UN chief put it this way: there may be no consensus in the negotiating room, but there is no ambiguity in the science.
So yes, the rules are hard. But the ozone deal was made by the same kind of countries, with the same kind of diplomats. So what made that one different?
Chapter two. The hole in the sky.
In nineteen eighty-five, three scientists at a station in Antarctica looked at their own numbers, and didn't believe them.
First, the shield. About fifteen to thirty-five kilometres above your head, there's a thin layer of ozone. It soaks up most of the sun's harshest ultraviolet light.
In nineteen seventy-four, two chemists, Mario Molina and Sherwood Rowland, warned that a group of chemicals called CFCs could drift up there and destroy it.
CFCs were everywhere. In spray cans, in fridges, in air conditioners, in foam. They seemed perfect. Cheap, safe to touch, and they never broke down. Which was exactly the problem.
Up high, sunlight finally breaks them apart, and each chlorine atom can destroy ozone again and again, thousands of times.

Then, in May nineteen eighty-five, Joe Farman, Brian Gardiner and Jonathan Shanklin of the British Antarctic Survey published their data. Every October, the ozone over their station at Halley was dropping. By about a third.
A hole, over Antarctica. And here's what happened next. Within two and a half years, the world signed a deal to fix it.
Chapter three. How the world said yes.
It wasn't because people were nicer in the eighties. It was because saying yes was cheap.
On the sixteenth of September, nineteen eighty-seven, the Montreal Protocol was agreed. A plan to cut CFCs, step by step.
First reason it worked: only a few companies made these chemicals. In the U S, there were five. And in nineteen eighty-eight, the biggest one, DuPont, said it would stop making them.
Second reason: replacements already existed, or were close. Your fridge still worked. Your deodorant still sprayed. Daily life barely changed.
Third reason: money. A fund was set up to help developing countries switch. So far, it has received pledges of over five billion dollars, and helped one hundred and forty-four countries.
And the treaty could be tightened, whenever the science got scarier. So it was. Again and again.
In two thousand and nine, the last country joined. Every country on Earth. Together with its parent treaty, it became the first global environmental agreement ever ratified by every country.
Today, nearly ninety-nine percent of the banned chemicals are gone. But here's the twist nobody expected.
Chapter four. The accidental climate treaty.
The ozone deal may have done more for the climate than any climate deal so far.
First, a myth. Many people think the ozone hole is what's heating the planet. It isn't. They're two different problems.
But they share some of the same culprits. CFCs don't just eat ozone. They're also powerful greenhouse gases, thousands of times stronger than carbon dioxide.

In twenty twenty-one, scientists modelled the world without the Montreal Protocol. By the end of this century, it would have been about two and a half degrees warmer, on top of the warming we already have.
Part of that comes from the gases themselves. And part comes from plants, burned by ultraviolet light, soaking up far less carbon.
Then, in twenty sixteen, in Kigali, the treaty grew again. It now also cuts HFCs, some of the gases that replaced CFCs. That could avoid up to half a degree of warming by twenty one hundred.
And the ozone layer itself? It's healing. Over most of the world, it should be back to nineteen-eighty levels around twenty forty. Over Antarctica, around twenty sixty-six.
So if the world can do this, why can't it do the same with carbon dioxide?
Chapter five. Why carbon is different.
To fix the ozone, we changed the gas in a fridge. To fix the climate, we'd have to change almost everything.
Coal, oil and gas still supply about eighty-six percent of the world's energy. They power cars, planes, factories, steel, cement, and the lights you're watching this by.
In twenty twenty-five, burning fossil fuels released a record thirty-eight billion tonnes of carbon dioxide. Not a few factories. Billions of chimneys and engines.

And there's a trap, described back in nineteen sixty-eight. It's called the tragedy of the commons. If everyone shares one field, each farmer gains by adding one more cow, and everyone shares the damage. The sky is that field.
The world first tried strict targets. In nineteen ninety-seven, the Kyoto Protocol set binding cuts for rich countries. The United States signed it, but never ratified it. Canada later walked out.
So in twenty fifteen, Paris tried the opposite. Every country picks its own plan. Almost everyone joined. Keep warming well below two degrees, and aim for one point five.
But add up those plans, and the U N's latest report says today's policies lead to about two point eight degrees by twenty one hundred.
So is it hopeless? Not quite. Because the ozone story has one more lesson.
Chapter six. Slow, but not stuck.
Consensus is slow. But history shows it isn't always stuck.
In twenty twenty-three, in Dubai, for the first time ever, nearly two hundred countries agreed on words they had avoided for almost thirty years: transitioning away from fossil fuels.
In the same year, the world agreed, by consensus, on a treaty to protect the high seas. It came into force in January twenty twenty-six.

And a myth worth fixing: twenty twenty-four was the first full year above one point five degrees. That doesn't mean the Paris goal is already lost. It's measured over twenty-year averages, and the long-term warming is still around one point three.
Remember why the ozone deal was easy: the alternatives were ready and cheap. The harder the change, the harder the yes. And the cheaper the change, the easier.
The next summit is in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, in November twenty twenty-seven. Same rules. Same hundred and ninety-odd voices.
So, why could the world fix one problem in the sky, but not the other?
Because the ozone deal asked a few factories to change one chemical, with replacements ready and money to help. The climate deal asks every country to change the energy under everything.
Same rules. Same people. A very different price of saying yes.

On Sunday night in Antalya, the summit ended without its main deal. And high above it, the hole the world agreed to fix in nineteen eighty-seven is quietly closing. Proof that the world can say yes. It has done it before.
